title: Truth, not eloquence (I.5)
hookLine: two printouts at a wedding lectern, one grand and one plain: chapter five says seek truth in scripture, not fine words
tomorrow: why would anyone say taking advice is safer than giving it?
last: DON'T BELIEVE IT, DON'T PASS IT ON.

cards: A cousin is asked to read at a wedding. At the lectern she has two printouts of the same passage. One is full of thee and thou and long rolling sentences.
The other reads like a text from a friend. Her hands are shaking a little. Which one is more true?
Chapter five of The Imitation of Christ would tell her the question is a good one, and the answer isn't about sound at all.

teach.b: Truth, not eloquence, is what to look for in holy scripture, the chapter says. Read it for what it gives you, not for fine phrasing. Read simple, devout books as gladly as lofty ones.

teach.h: MARK WHAT IS SAID, NOT WHO.
teach.b: And then the line worth repeating to a friend tonight: don't ask who said it; mark what is said. Don't be swayed by a writer's reputation, great learning or small. Let love of plain truth draw you to read.

teach.h: THE TRUTH OF THE LORD REMAINETH.
teach.b: Because people pass away, but, quoting a psalm, as the Douay-Rheims puts it: "the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever." God speaks in many ways, the chapter says, and without favoring anyone.
Then a gentle warning about ourselves. Curiosity often gets in the way, it says, when we try to pick apart and argue over what we should simply take in and move past.
So the counsel is three plain words: read humbly, simply, faithfully. And don't wish to be known as learned. That loops back to chapter two, love to be unknown.
For the cousin at the lectern, the grand version and the plain one can carry the same truth. What matters is that the people listening can hear it.

how: At Mass, Catholics hear scripture read aloud from the Lectionary in a translation the Church approves; at home, some read whichever faithful translation they understand, slowly, for what it says.

games.q: in your book club, one member won't read a saint's little book because the author "wasn't a real scholar." what does chapter five say?
o: don't ask who said it; mark what is said.
only read authors with impressive credentials.
skip every book except scripture itself.
games.why: the Imitation says don't be moved by a writer's learning, great or small: let the love of plain truth draw you to read.

practice: Say one short line aloud, plainly, no performance voice, the way you'd tell a friend something true. The psalm's line works: the truth of the Lord remaineth for ever. Say it once more, slower, and let the plain words stay with you.

wordCard.voice: Truth. What chapter five says to seek in scripture: not fine words, not well-known names, but what is said.
